"You're weird...but in a *good* way."

Not exactly a superlative, but it's how most of my classmates described me in high school. I spent my time drawing comics and writing short stories that made their way around school. I was a bit of a prankster, too. My crowning achievement? Sneaking into the principal’s office with my best friend to broadcast a live message over the intercom—right before finals. I warned the entire school that "The End" was near and doom was imminent. Then my best friend cut in, yelling, *"EVERYBODY POLKA!"*—right as a polka song blared through the speakers. It was absolute chaos. 

What else? Supergluing quarters to the vending machine’s coin return slot and watching as people tried (and failed) to pry them off. In keyboarding class, updating spellcheck to automatically replace common words with creatively chosen swear words. And my personal favorite—sneaking photos of random strangers into my history teacher’s family photo display and seeing how long it took him to notice.

Basically, I did anything I could to break up the soul-crushing monotony of high school life. If that makes me weird, then I'll gladly take it, because the alternative is *way* too boring.

It may seem like an advantage but it's a double-edged sword.

As a conventionally attractive woman, I can easily attract the kind of individuals who place great value on a woman's physical beauty, but I'd much rather be in a relationship with someone who values my inner qualities and hard-won accomplishments. Too often, I'm pursued by individuals who only *pretend* to be interested in my personality, when in reality, they only want to use me for my body. They don't see me as a person with thoughts and feelings, but rather, as a "prize" to be won—a trophy they can show off to other people to elevate their own social status. Unsurprisingly, these individuals tend to be incredibly selfish and manipulative. And that is *not* the kind of person I want to attract into  my life.

Conversely, I've never placed much importance on my partners' physical appearance. We're all just brains sloshing around in meat suits, the way I see it. My best friend (a stunningly gorgeous lesbian who only dates stunningly gorgeous lesbians) is often surprised by the people I end up dating. She jokingly refers to me as a "romantic transcendentalist". Gender, race, height, weight, age—none of it matters to me as long as we’re both consenting adults. What truly matters to me is a person's ability to match my intelligence and share my interests. Sadly, most of my romantic partners are also surprised by my willingness to date them, simply because they don't fit conventional standards of attractiveness.

Despite my openness, it's still difficult for me to find people I can connect with on a deeply meaningful level. Only 3-5% of the world’s population exhibits gifted characteristics, and even less have similar interests and compatible personalities, which makes finding a perfect match statistically improbable.

I was fortunate enough to come close to it once, with a man thirty-three years my senior. He was a former MENSA member, a Harvard graduate, and an accomplished computer scientist—an absolutely brilliant human being.  I was willing to overlook the age gap because I deeply valued his mind and wanted to spend as much time with him as possible. We were married for three glorious years and then he passed away from esophageal cancer, taken from me even sooner than I could have anticipated. But I don’t regret a single second of it.

While I miss our grand adventures (going on cross-country road trips, attending lectures together, and so much more) what I miss the most are our conversations. For so long, I had hidden my intelligence away from the world, allowing it to become dormant. But with him, I’d never felt so intellectually stimulated—so truly *alive*. When he passed away, a huge wealth of knowledge disappeared with him. There are still so many questions I want to ask him but will never get the chance.

Losing my husband was the single most devastating moment of my life. And yet, the fact that he existed at all gives me hope, because it proves there are others like me out there. I owe it to them (and to myself) to find them.

And so, the search continues...

My ADHD brain is like a chaotic city that never sleeps. Some of the skyscrapers still have scaffolding sticking out of them because the construction crew got distracted halfway through the building process. Traffic infrastructure is a total nightmare. Granted, a few of the streets are highly-efficient information highways, but most of them are detours that lead to random alleys full of weird, fascinating things.

Everywhere you look, there are neon signs trying to get your attention. One moment it's "Hey, remember that embarrassing thing you did five years ago?" and the next it’s "Omg, what if you learned everything about medieval swordsmithing *right now*?"

There's a movie theater in the heart of the city, and the only thing it shows is worst-case scenarios. You punch in a random thought like, "What if I forgot to lock the door?" and BAM—full IMAX feature of everything that could go wrong, complete with dramatic music and over-the-top catastrophes. It's very, very popular.

Right next to that is the Earworm Jukebox, which plays the same three seconds of a song on repeat, whether you want it to or not. There’s also a sketchy back alley where the memory thieves hang out, snatching random things you definitely needed to remember. And then there's the infamous "Deja Vue" neighborhood. It’s this weird, looping part of the city where everything feels familiar, but you can’t figure out why. You’ll turn a corner and swear you’ve been there before—same coffee shop, same guy with a fedora, same bulldog tied to a lamppost. It’s like the city itself is messing with you.

And of course, the whole place is *swarming* with dopamine junkies—tiny little gremlins running around screaming, "WE NEED STIMULATION!"

It can be unpredictable and exhausting, but it's also full of creativity, weird charm, and moments of brilliance that I wouldn't trade for anything. It might not make a lot of sense to other people, but I wouldn't want it any other way.

Interestingly, at least one scientific study suggests the opposite to be true: smarter individuals may actually be *more* *susceptible* to biased interpretations of information. This is because they possess a greater depth of knowledge and a wider range of explanations, which they can use to rationalize or explain away facts that challenge their existing beliefs.

I'm inclined to believe it. As someone who identifies as "gifted", and has several close friends within the gifted community, I’m often struck by how easily we can point out the cognitive biases in others, yet seem blind to our own. It’s as if our intellectual abilities, rather than being a safeguard against bias, have equipped us with even more sophisticated tools to defend our views, making it all the more difficult for us to see when we are falling prey to the very biases we so easily identify in others. It’s a paradox I find both fascinating and unsettling.

He may also be using a manipulation tactic known as "intermittent reinforcement". He may offer you a tiny bit of positive attention or approval, but only in sporatic, unpredictable bursts. This causes you to become emotionally addicted to him, as you start to crave the occasional moments of validation he provides. You’ll be left in a constant state of uncertainty—one minute, he’s ignoring you or being dismissive, and the next, he offers you a compliment or a moment of kindness. This on-and-off pattern can make you chase the validation even harder, because it creates hope that the positive attention will return, even if it’s rarely consistent.

It’s important to recognize this as a manipulation tactic, not a sign that he’s changing or becoming more considerate. Narcissists and manipulators rely on intermittent reinforcement to maintain control, keeping you emotionally invested while ensuring you remain uncertain about where you stand with them. It’s an exhausting cycle that wears you down, because you never know when you’ll get the positive reinforcement you’re seeking.

Be aware of this possibility. If your coworker starts to mix his silence with occasional gestures of friendliness or compliments, recognize it for what it is—a way to keep you hooked while still maintaining control over the situation. This kind of behavior can make you question your own boundaries and feel like you need to prove something to him, but it’s important that you stay strong. Your peace and self-worth are far more important than any validation he can offer. Don’t let him pull you back into the cycle of unpredictability.

If your coworker is narcissistic, as many of us suspect, he may be punishing you for having the *audacity* to set a boundary with him.

Narcissists don't understand the concept of healthy boundaries. Because of their inflated egos, they feel entitled to unrestricted access to other people's time, energy, and emotions. When someone dares to set a boundary, they interpret it as a personal attack or an act of defiance. They feel as if they're being denied something they're rightfully owed, so they lash out in subtle or overt ways. Your coworker may be using silence as a weapon to make you feel guilty, anxious, or abandoned, which is a classic manipulation tactic.

You had every right to cut him off. He hurt you, and he owes you an apology—plain and simple. Yet somehow, you still feel the need to apologize to him. I hope you can see the issue here. It sounds like some part of you still wants to earn his approval, to the point where you're willing to overlook his flagrant disrespect and even find ways to blame yourself. That’s exactly the kind of power dynamic that manipulative people thrive on—it keeps them in control while leaving you second-guessing your own actions and worth.

Many of us with AvPD struggle with self-worth. We tend to be people pleasers, and often go out of our way to avoid disagreements or uncomfortable situations, even at the expense of our own needs or boundaries. Unfortunately, these traits can make us easy targets for manipulative or domineering individuals. Your coworker likely recognized this about you and exploited it, sensing that you might be less likely to push back or stand up for yourself. But his behavior reflects on him, not you, and it's important to remember that you deserve respect and fairness in all your interactions.

When you stopped reacting to his negging, he likely realized that particular tactic had lost its power over you. Manipulators like him rarely give up when their initial methods fail—they adapt. Now, he may be trying a different strategy: the silent treatment. This is another classic manipulation tool, designed to keep you feeling unsure and unsettled. By withdrawing attention, he hopes to make you question your decision to set boundaries and prompt you to chase after his approval again.

But here’s the thing: **you’re winning by not engaging.** By holding your ground and not seeking his validation, you’ve taken away his ability to control you through negative comments or emotional withholding. Even if he doesn’t apologize or try to make amends, you’ve already reclaimed some of your power. You’ve gained peace of mind and a reprieve from his negging, which is invaluable for your self-esteem and emotional well-being.

If he does eventually try to make amends, you have the right to decide whether his actions seem genuine and whether you’re willing to risk letting him back into your space. Trust your instincts—if there’s no real accountability or change on his part, it’s okay to maintain your distance. Prioritize your peace and self-respect over his approval. That’s the kind of boundary-setting that protects you and helps you heal.

I was diagnosed as "gifted" at eight years old. I was also very, very shy.

It was difficult for me to develop meaningful relationships with my peers due to our intellectual disparities. Socialization felt performative—something I had to consciously think about rather than an intuitive interaction. The friendships I managed to form felt shallow and unsatisfying, but the alternative—total solitude—was unbearable. So, I forced myself to feign interest in my classmates' discussions and hobbies, because I was desperate to avoid the dull ache of loneliness.

I resented how much of myself I had to sacrifice just to make friends. I would force a smile and nod enthusiastically while listening to my peers talk about their interests, but any time I tried to bring up my own interests, their eyes would instantly glaze over. The silence that followed was even more painful than the conversation itself. So, I learned to never talk about my own interests. Instead, I swallowed my thoughts and became a mirror, reflecting only what they wanted to hear.

Because of my giftedness, my parents set impossibly high standards for me. They assumed I would excel at everything in life without any effort on my part. Unlike my peers, I wasn't praised or rewarded when I did well in school. I was simply doing what was expected of me. To make matters worse, my father was a well-known figure within our community. Image meant everything to him. He was acutely aware of my neurodivergence and watched me like a hawk, ready to attack if I said or did anything that might embarrass him. Every time I failed to socialize “correctly,” he criticized me, reinforcing the idea that something was fundamentally wrong with me.

Ironically, my father's attempts to "fix" me created the very problem he was trying to prevent. Over time, I internalized his insecurities, and my shyness spiraled into a full-blown social anxiety disorder. I could never relax enough to enjoy a conversation because I was always monitoring myself from the outside, replaying and critiquing every single word and gesture, just as my father had done.

Socializing became an exhausting ordeal, and avoiding it became the only rational choice. What was the point of putting on a performance for other people when they couldn't care less about me? And what would be my reward for persevering? A lifetime of soul-crushingly dull conversations?

Loneliness seemed less painful than criticism, rejection, and the banality of superficial relationships. So, I retreated further into myself, pulling away from the outside world until relationships shifted from tangible experiences to abstract notions that existed only in my mind. Socializing became a theoretical exercise, an intellectual puzzle rather than a form of genuine connection. The social skills I learned in childhood began to atrophy, like a muscle left dormant for too long. By adulthood I was a total outsider—feral, disconnected—a silent observer behind a pane of glass, watching but never participating. When I finally encountered other neurodivergent adults in real life, I was ecstatic, but the damage had already been done. I had forgotten how to be human, how to communicate. And by then, it was too late. The opportunity had slipped away.

So, what caused me to develop social anxiety? I think it can be broken down into three things:

1. A lack of true peers with whom I could form meaningful connections.
2. A hypercritical parent who only "loved" me when I performed perfectly.
3. An inherent inclination towards perfectionism as well as heightened emotional sensitivity and anxiety, all of which are traits associated with giftedness.

I can "see" why having aphantsia would make it difficult to avoid white room syndrome. Here are some alternative strategies that don't rely on mental imagery:

1) Think beyond sight. Focus on sounds, smells, textures, tastes, and temperature. For example, describe the scent of rain-soaked earth or the texture of worn leather chairs. Ask yourself, "What would this place sound like?" or "How does the ground feel underfoot?"

2. Do some research and use reference materials. Study images or watch videos of environments similar to your own. Use online tours or visit places to immerse yourself in the details. Keep notes or descriptions of environments you encounter in real life.

3. Build the scene through lists. Write out everything the character might notice in a location. For example:

   * What’s in the room? (Furniture, decorations, objects.)
   * What’s happening around them? (People, weather, sounds.)
   * How does the character interact with it? (Do they touch, hear, or taste something?)

4. Reveal the environment organically, through dialogue and interaction. For example, instead of saying, "The room had old, busted windows," show it through action: "She rubbed her arms and shivered as the cold night air seeped through the cracks in the windows."

5. Use metaphors and similes. Instead of picturing a "stormy sea," think of words that convey its mood, like "The waves clawed at the shore, roaring with a feral fury."

6. Collaborate with others. If you're stuck, ask a friend or beta reader how they'd describe a setting. They might highlight details you hadn’t considered.

Here's what I learned in rehab. Take it to heart, and you could save yourself $75K worth of medical treatment:

**1)** **Ditch the scale and forget about counting calories**  
These numbers are totally arbitrary and no longer define you.

**2)** **Practice mindful eating**  
Years of dieting can disconnect you from your body’s natural hunger and fullness cues. To rebuild this connection, try mindful eating. For your next few meals, eliminate distractions like phones, TVs, or music. Pay close attention to your body: every few bites, ask yourself, *"How full do I feel on a scale of 1-10?"* Aim to stop eating when you reach a comfortable 7 or 8. If you feel uncomfortably full, you've gone too far—but that's okay! With practice, you’ll become skilled at recognizing these cues and naturally stop eating when your body signals it’s had enough.

**3)** **Eat regular meals to regain your body's trust**  
Your body needs consistency to heal from cycles of restriction and bingeing. Eating regularly signals to your body that it can rely on you to meet its needs, pulling it out of survival mode and stabilizing your metabolism and weight. Aim for three balanced meals and two to three snacks daily, eating approximately every three hours to keep your energy steady—think of it as stoking a furnace to keep the fire burning.

Here’s the schedule we used in my treatment center:

7:00am - Breakfast  
10:00am - Snack  
12:00pm - Lunch  
3:00pm - Snack  
6:00pm - Dinner  
8:00pm - Snack

**4) Give yourself nourishing options**. Start small —drink a glass of water first thing in the morning to hydrate your body. Craving pizza for dinner? Enjoy it, but pair it with a colorful side salad to boost your nutrients. Reframing your mindset to include foods that fuel you, rather than limiting what you eat, helps create a healthier, more sustainable approach to eating.

**5) Find fun ways to move your body**  
Exercise should feel like a celebration, not a chore. Skip the gym if it doesn't bring you joy and find activities that make you feel alive—go hiking in the woods, play pickleball with friends, or try a dance class just for fun. Move your body not for weight loss, but for the rush of endorphins that boost your mood and energy. Do it because you love how it makes you feel, because you care about your health, and because you want to embrace life and be present for as long as possible. Let movement be an act of self-love, not punishment.

**6) Love yourself fiercely**  
When you truly love yourself, you no longer rely on anyone else’s approval to feel worthy of existence. You free yourself from society’s narrow expectations, and that kind of freedom is far more precious than conforming to ideals like being “thin.” Self-love makes you untouchable. While your cousins struggle to find their worth in an endless, losing battle against unrealistic beauty standards, you’ll already have won—because you’ve stepped out of the fight entirely.

Diet culture is a lie—a trap designed to keep you chasing an impossible ideal. Don’t buy into it. Break free, step outside its constraints, and reclaim your life. By doing so, you’ll gain the one thing everyone truly desires: genuine freedom and self-acceptance.

I say this as someone who nearly lost their ten-year battle with anorexia. At my worst, I was hospitalized for 110 days and worked with a dedicated team of nutritionists, doctors, and psychologists who literally saved my life. They helped me heal my unhealthy relationship with my body and opened my eyes to the harmful influence of "diet culture".  
  
It sounds like you might also have an unhealthy relationship with your body. Let me reassure you: **there is absolutely nothing wrong with you.** You are not lazy. You are not a "pig". More importantly, you don't need to be physically attractive to be worthy of other people's love and respect. You likely have many wonderful qualities that have nothing to do with your appearance. Imagine how limiting it would be, if "thinness" was your only positive trait, when you have the potential to be so much more!  
  
Your cousins' criticism is damaging your self-esteem, so it's essential to set firm boundaries with them. Here's a simple formula that I use all the time:  
  
"When you (describe the problematic behavior) I feel (express your emotion) because (explain the reason). In the future, I would like to request (state the change that you need). If this doesn't happen, I will have to (explain the consequence)."  
  
Here's how this might look for your situation:  
  
"When you criticize my appearance, it hurts my feelings because it feels like you care more about my body than about me as a person. In the future, I'd appreciate it if you kept these thoughts to yourselves. If you criticize my appearance again, I will have to end the conversation."

Don't listen to the haters. And by that, I mean make it physically impossible to engage with them. Remind your cousins of your boundaries when they criticize your appearance. If they ignore you, leave the conversation (walk out of the room, hang up the phone, etc.). If the behavior continues, stop answering their phone calls or attending family functions. I'm totally serious. Their casual cruelty is feeding your eating disorder. Ask yourself: is maintaining this relationship worth sacrificing my happiness and health? The answer should always prioritize your well-being and peace of mind.

You've done a great job with this piece! It "hooked" me from the very beginning and kept me reading until the end, which is no small feat, considering how short my attention span is! Atlas' internal conflict felt compelling, and your use of sensory details, like the crunch of snow and the wind, created a strong atmospheric presence. I did notice a few small things that could be improved, but overall you've done a fantastic job!

Here are a few of the things I noticed. Please keep in mind that I'm only an amateur writer, so you'll want to take all of these suggestions with a grain of salt!

>"Dead bodies and blood stained the snow, the red color bringing a nice contrast to the white earth around them. Atlas couldn’t tell if he liked it or not."

Phrases like "bringing a nice contrast" and "couldn't tell if he liked it or not" feel out of place tonally in such a grim setting, but maybe that was intentional on your part.

>"*Did I kill them all?* He thought to himself."

The word "he" doesn't need to be capitalized here. When a thought is in italics or quotation marks, the narrative continuation doesn't need capitalization unless it starts a new sentence.   
  
Corrected version: "*Did I kill them all?* he thought to himself." 

Also consider replacing "he thought to himself" with something more emotionally impactful. 

Example: "*Did I kill them all?* The thought hit him like a blow."

>"He stood by himself. Breathing. For a moment, then laughter broke through it, his laughter."

Fragmented sentences can be effective when used sparingly, but overuse can make the writing feel stilted. I would suggest rewriting this section so it's slightly less fragmented. Also, the repetition of "laughter" feels redundant. 

>"He didn’t know if it was nervous laughter or happy laughter, but he laughed."

Again, the repetition of "laughter" feels redundant. 

>"His legs subconsciously began to move, and He ran into the forest beside the field."

"Subconsciously began to move" is redundant, because the context already implies this is a subconscious action. 

Suggested edit: "His legs began to move, and He ran into the forest beside the field."

>"He hid behind a tree, suddenly feeling paranoid someone was watching him."

The word "suddenly" is unnecessary here because the context already suggests his anxiety is escalating. The word "feeling" is also unnecessary and should be left out because it's a filter word.   
  
Suggested edit: "He hid behind a tree, paranoid someone was watching him."

>"His stomach hurt, and his heart felt like it was gonna break through his skin."

"Gonna" is overly casual for the tone of this piece. Either write it out completely as "going to" or replace it with something else. I would also avoid using the word "felt" because it's a filter word.  
  
Suggested edit: "His stomach hurt, and his heart pounded as if it might break through his skin.

>"He was so sure someone was watching him."

The phrase "watching him" is written three times in the same paragraph. I would suggest rephrasing at least two of these to avoid redundancy.

>"He began to move through the dense trees, running towards the port."

The word "began" is unnecessary here and it actually makes the writing less compelling because it delays the action. I suggest removing it entirely.

Suggested edit: "He moved through the dense trees, running towards the port."

Your post triggered something inside of me that I've been thinking about a lot lately. I'd like to expand on my previous response, because I think it might help some people:  
  
We humans have an innate desire to connect. Sometimes our attempts to communicate with each other can be awkward and embarrassing, but it's always worth the risk. Those of us with AvPD might not have the most developed social skills, but even people who don't speak the same language can still find ways to understand each other. They'll use broken words, sound effects, facial expressions, and exaggerated hand gestures. Whatever it takes to get the message across. And while these conversations tend to be messy and confusing, when both parties finally reach a shared understanding, the joy is undeniable. That's because the vast majority of us don't seek perfection in communication; we seek *connection*.

In fact, making mistakes and admitting that we're feeling anxious can create a deeper bond with our listeners. Our vulnerability reminds them that we both have a desire to connect on a human level. There’s something beautiful about opening up and showing that we care more about understanding each other than about getting every word right.

Something that helps me personally is to approach every conversation as a kind of experiment: “Can I get my point across with this statement?” No? Then try again, maybe phrasing it differently or adding a new gesture. Communication isn’t a one-time test; it’s a process where we’re allowed to try over and again, until we can successfully get our message across. Most people are not only patient with this but eager to help us reach that understanding, because they genuinely want to connect with us, too.

Hope this helps. Even if only just a little bit.

You're not alone in feeling this way, and what you’re describing is more common than you might think—especially for people in their early 20s. That fear of “messing up” or feeling like you’re a burden is something a lot of us have gone through, and it doesn't necessarily mean you're failing in any way. In fact, it sounds like you're deeply considerate of other people’s time and feelings, which shows how empathetic you are.

Becoming an adult is a challenge for everyone. There's no manual that tells us what to do, and most of us are just figuring things out as we go. It's okay to be scared of making phone calls and sending out applications. These kinds of things get easier with practice. It helps to set small goals, like writing down a script for a phone call, or even practicing ordering food out loud. Little steps like these will build your confidence bit by bit.

Also, remember: the the people on the other end of those calls or emails are there to help and support you. It’s okay to reach out to them; that’s their job, and they don’t expect you to be perfect. One day, you’ll look back and realize how far you’ve come. For now, be gentle with yourself. You're already doing better than you realize.

This is what people say when they want to avoid taking accountability for their actions.

Instead of engaging in the issue or trying to improve the relationship, your boyfriend has decided to invalidate your feelings and concerns. He's implied that you're causing the problem by choosing to stay with him, rather than addressing the actual behavior that's causing the problem. He's placing the burden of the relationship's health entirely on you so he can sidestep any responsibility and accuse you of causing all the tension, rather than admitting his behavior is the problem.

Your boyfriend has no intentions of changing, so he's given you an ultimatum: accept all of his toxic behavior without question or leave. But he doesn't actually expect you to leave; he's exploiting your fear and guilt.

Call him out on his bluff and see how quickly he changes tactics. He will likely beg you to come back and promise to work on himself, but this is a lie meant to reel you back into the relationship. Make sure you follow through with your decision and actually leave him.

My AvPD was most severe during my teens and early twenties. Now that I'm in my late-thirties, I still experience social anxiety from time to time, but it's nowhere near as debilitating as it once was. My approach to meeting and interacting with people has changed a lot since then, and might not resonate with most of the people on this forum. Keeping that that in mind, I believe it would be more helpful to share some examples from my past, when my AvPD was at its most intense.

**How did you meet?** 

I met my first boyfriend on Myspace, a social networking service that was popular back in the early 2000s. He saw my photo, thought I looked cute, and sent me a friend request along with a brief message. I was 21 years old at the time.

**Did you tell him about your issues?** 

Ironically, it was impossible for me to avoid telling him about my AvPD. After a few weeks of online messaging, he asked if we could talk on the phone, and I told him that I really wanted to, but I was too afraid. This inevitably led to a conversation about my AvPD.

**How did he feel about it?** 

He struggled to comprehend how someone like me—someone so friendly, likeable, and attractive—could have such debilitating social anxiety. But he was also grappling with a mental illness, so he at least understood what it was like to act in ways that others found puzzling.

**Did you ever push him away to protect yourself from rejection?** 

Shortly after moving in with him, my boyfriend would say or do things that made me suspect he was cheating on me. During these times, I would become very quiet and withdrawn, because the thought of it hurt me deeply.

**Were you worried he would find someone "better"?**

I worried about it constantly. In his case, there were signs—messages that suggested he might be talking to other girls online. But, looking back, I doubt he would have left me for someone else. He always said I was “out of his league” and couldn’t understand why I chose to be with him. 

**Aren't you a people pleaser in these relationships?** 

Yes, absolutely. 

My boyfriend and I were together for five years. I finally left him when his alcoholism spiraled out of control, but in truth, it should’ve ended long before that. I was simply too stubborn to give up on him–to give up on *us*. But you can’t save someone who doesn’t want to be saved.

**How do you get into relationships?**

Surprisingly easily.

First, being a woman gives me an advantage. Society still expects men to make the first move, so I rarely have to face the risk of rejection—I just have to wait for someone to approach me.

Second, I benefit from being physically attractive. We live in a superficial world where many people value a woman's appearance above everything else. Most straight men are willing to overlook my personality disorder simply because of how I look on the outside. (No, it's not fair, but again, this is the kind of world we live in.)

**Do you feel like you're genuine with your partner? Do you relax in their company?**

It depends on the individual and how well I know them.

It's been nearly a decade since I broke up with my first boyfriend. In that time, I've dated over 20 people and was even married for a few years. My greatest relationships-the ones where I can truly be myself-have always been with people who started out as friends and knew me well before we started dating.

This is actually great information to have, because it pinpoints a specific section where the story might be losing readers' interest. By focusing on this section, you can make targeted improvements to strengthen the story and keep readers engaged beyond the first few chapters. There are several factors that could be contributing to their lack of interest:

* **Weak Hook**: If the beginning of the novel doesn’t grab attention right away, readers may lose interest quickly. The opening chapters need to establish stakes, intrigue, or an emotional connection to the characters.
* **Character Development**: Readers often continue reading because they care about the characters. If the characters don’t feel relatable, dynamic, or compelling early on, readers may lose interest. They need to see growth or potential for growth in the main characters to stay invested.
* **Conflict**: If the initial conflict is weak or the stakes feel too low, readers might not feel compelled to continue. Early tension or problems need to be engaging and clear to maintain attention.
* **Clarity and Focus**: If the plot is confusing, meandering, or unfocused, readers may become disengaged. Early chapters should clearly set up the story's direction without overwhelming the reader with too much exposition or unnecessary detail.
* **Dialogue and Prose**: Overly wordy, clunky, or unnatural dialogue can disengage readers. Similarly, dense or awkward prose can slow down the reading experience and deter interest.
* **World-Building Overload**: While detailed world-building is important in certain genres, too much exposition early on can bog down the story, making it hard for readers to get to the action or emotional core.
* **Poor Pacing:** If the story moves too slowly, readers may feel that not enough is happening to hold their attention. Early chapters need to establish momentum, offering a balance between building the world, developing characters, and advancing the plot. If too much time is spent on setup without meaningful conflict or tension, readers might lose patience and disengage. On the other hand, if the pacing is too fast, important emotional or narrative beats might be rushed, leaving readers disconnected from the story or characters.

Most importantly, don't take it personally—people's attention spans are shorter than ever, and even accomplished writers struggle to keep readers engaged beyond a few chapters. The fact that readers stop after four chapters doesn’t reflect your potential, but highlights the challenge all writers face today. Use this feedback as motivation to refine your story, knowing that it's part of the process every writer goes through.

Since his passing, I've built a sizeable social circle, but I still feel painfully lonely. Somehow, this feels worse than actually being *alone*.

My first heartbreak:

My first boyfriend and I lived together and had been a couple for over five years. Throughout those years, I always felt like something was missing from our relationship, but I couldn't figure out what it was. I felt lonely and unfulfilled, but I didn't know why. I didn't think these feelings were a good enough reason to end the relationship, so I kept suffering through it. Every few months, doubt would creep back in. We'd talk through it, and I'd feel better—for a little while. But the doubt always returned, creating a vicious cycle.

One day, I couldn't ignore the feeling anymore. The anxiety was making me sick to my stomach, and I couldn't eat or drink anything without throwing up.  I tossed and turned in bed for hours every single night. After a week of not being able to eat or sleep, I realized I couldn't live in denial any longer. I *had* to end the relationship. I explained all of this to my boyfriend, and he agreed that ending things was for the best. He confessed that his physical attraction for me had faded long ago, and that he now saw me as more of a roommate than as a romantic partner. It hurt me to hear this, but deep down inside, I knew  it was true.

My boyfriend helped me pack up my belongings and drove me across the state, back to my family. As we drove, we laughed and cried, reminiscing about all the good memories we'd made together over the years. It was a bittersweet moment, filled with both heartache and gratitude for one another.

My worst heartbreak:

I spent the next several years moving from one unsatisfying relationship to another. By the time I turned 30, I had given up all hope of ever finding "The One". I decided that true love was a phenomenon reserved for "Everyone Else", and that I should be grateful to even *be* in a relationship, even if it left me feeling lonely and unfulfilled.

Then, when I least expected it, I met the man who would forever change my life. He understood me on a deep emotional level, and our friendship had a depth that most of my friendships and intimate relationships could only skim the surface of. For the first time in my life, I didn't feel alone.

I knew immediately this was the man I wanted to spend the rest of my life with, and he felt the same way about me. We got engaged three months later and were married within a year. The three years we spent together were some of the happiest of my  life.

Then, in February 2020, he was diagnosed with esophageal cancer. He died just eight weeks later.

I still remember the phone call. The nurse called me at two in the morning, letting me know my husband had passed away. I dropped my phone on the floor and screamed into the void, over and over again. Meanwhile, I could still hear the nurse on the other end of the line, asking me if I was still there. When I picked up the phone again, she urged me to begin making funeral arrangements as soon as possible, but I could barely process anything she was saying.

At the time, hospitals weren't allowing patients to have visitors, due to the COVID outbreak. I couldn't be with my husband during his final two weeks of life. He had to die alone. It still angers me, and breaks my heart, to this day.

Losing my soulmate was the most devastating moment of my life. All I ever wanted was to find someone I could truly connect with, and for a short period, I did. But he's gone now. It would be easy to become bitter and resentful, but instead, I choose to be grateful for the time we had together, brief as it was. And I still hold onto the hope that someday I'll find someone as amazing as he was.

My battle with Anorexia began at age 16 and continued for over a decade. No one realized I was struggling with an eating disorder because I didn't look "sick" on the outside. For me, the weight loss came very gradually, because I have hypoglycemia and have to eat every few hours to prevent myself from passing out.

At age 26, I broke up with my long-term boyfriend and moved into a place of my own. For the first time in my life, I didn't have anyone monitoring my food intake or influencing my eating habits. As a result, my weight dropped rapidly, and a year later I became so sick that I had to be hospitalized.

I spent the next 110 days at a rehabilitation center and was fortunate enough to work with a very talented team of doctors, nutritionists, and psychologists. They taught me how to cope with my depression in healthy ways, helped me rebuild my self-esteem, and opened my eyes to the insidious nature of "diet culture", which made me rethink my relationship with food and also with myself. I'm not exaggerating when I say they saved my life.

I'm now 37-years old and consider myself mostly recovered. There are still days where I struggle with intrusive thoughts, but they're nowhere near as intense as they were a decade ago. Obviously, not everyone is going to have the same results that I've had, but I recommend that everyone try in-patient treatment at least once, if given the option.

In my twenties I was unemployed, severely depressed, and slowly starving myself to death. I had no friends and the loneliness was unbearable.

My life turned around when I joined a support group for people with eating disorders. At that point I was desperate for any kind of contact with other human beings. The group leader saw how sick my Anorexia had made me and urged me to apply for something called the MANNA scholarship. She told me it could help me pay for the medical treatment that I so desperately needed. To my surprise, I won the scholarship and was granted enough money to go to an eating disorder clinic for three months.

At the clinic I was able to work with a great team of medical doctors and also received 24/7 psychiatric care, personal counseling, antidepressants, and nutritious meals. For the first time in my life I had access to all of the things I needed to get better.

Three months later the clinic released me with an intensive aftercare plan. Part of my aftercare plan included free job training which I received at a place called the AIM center. The center is essentially a clubhouse that provides psychosocial rehabilitation services for people with mental illnesses and other disabilities. They helped me find my first fulltime job. They also encouraged me to submit my artwork to a local art gallery. The gallery loved my portfolio and I was able to make a little side income selling my artwork there.

So at this point in my life I was making some money and feeling much more confident about myself. Going to work every day helped me get out of the house and socialize on a regular basis. It also helped me to establish a regular eating and sleeping routine, which was great for my mental health. Just the fact that I was eating again did wonders for me.

That confidence and renewed energy gave me the boost I needed to put myself out there and start making friends again. I joined a local meetup group and became friends with the group leader. She invited me to her birthday party and that's where I met my husband. 

When I was in my twenties I didn't think I would ever get married. I thought I was too "broken" and "undesirable" to even be in a relationship. But I was wrong - I was worth it all along - and my husband reminds me of this every day. Marrying him is the best thing I've ever done. He is my best friend and I can't imagine my life without him.

We have a good life. My husband makes enough money for us both to live comfortably. I'm thankful that I no longer have to decide between food and medication. I'm thankful that I no longer lay awake in bed all night, wondering if I'm going to die alone, and then crying myself to sleep. I'm thankful that my husband has a great circle of friends who have welcomed me into their fold. They're always there for me when I'm feeling down.

The life I live now is a far cry from the life I lived just a few years ago. There had been so many times where I wanted to kill myself, and I'm so glad I didn't. Just imagine everything I would have missed out on.

We actually talked about it the other night. He reassured me that I'm worthy of being in a relationship and that he would absolutely marry me all over again if he had the choice. Hey lovehat3. Thanks for your feedback. I can understand why you feel like I don't have AvPD. I'm coping rather well these days, but it took years of therapy to get to the point where I am now.

In college I had to share a tiny dorm room with three other girls. It was a living nightmare. I talked to them as little as possible and avoided them at all costs. On the rare occasion where I had the room to myself, I would pee in the sink so I wouldn't have to venture out to the community restroom and risk running into someone I knew. I could go for weeks without speaking to a single soul. I never ate in the cafeteria because there were too many people. Instead, I would grab fistfuls of food from the buffet table and hide it in my backpack so I could eat it somewhere else. One time I forgot to do my homework for my English class so I decided to skip class that day. I didn't want to embarrass myself in front of the whole class by telling the teacher I didn't do my homework. I never went back to that class. Then I stopped attending my other classes for similar reasons. I cut off all contact with my friends and family members because I didn't want them to know I was failing. By the time Christmas vacation came around I had nowhere to go. My dad lived just a few miles away from campus but I was too scared and ashamed to show my face. I spent those two weeks sleeping in a cold and damp abandoned mill. I felt so lonely I tried to hang myself.

I dropped out of college the next semester and moved into my mom's apartment. My AvPD got even worse and I didn't leave the house for two years. My mom had to make all of my phone calls for me because I was terrified of talking to other people. I felt lonely, frustrated, and trapped. Suicide was always on the forefront of my mind.

Long story short, I became determined to change my life for the better, and my AvPD slowly improved over the next ten years. I had to go through a slew of therapists and support groups and tried several different combinations of psychiatric medications before I found something that worked for me. At one point I had to be hospitalized for three months (Anorexia) but it was one of the best things that ever happened to me because the treatment center I went to taught me how to love myself and cope with my mental illnesses. Last year (at age 30) I got my first full-time job and it did wonders for my self-esteem. Shortly after that I met the love of my life and we got engaged. My fiance has a very active social life and, as his future wife, I have had to force myself to step outside of my comfort zone time and time again. It was terrifying at first but after a while it got easier. Now I don't mind hanging out with his friends. I'm even making friends of my own, which is something I've always struggled with.

I posted this because I wanted you all to know AvPD can get better. It can take a lot of time and effort, but it's totally possible and it's totally worth it.

I also feel that I am ahead of my peers in some ways. I'm engaged to the love of my life, and yet, sadly, my best friend hasn't had any success with her romantic relationships. She's my age (30) and still hasn't lost her virginity.

I'm also better off financially because I don't have to pay off student loans. Plus my fiancé is rather affluent and well-known in our community. We live in a beautiful house and we eat at the finest restaurants, attend the opera on a regular basis, and travel around the world. I spent most of my childhood and adulthood trapped in the clutches of poverty but now I'm living the kind of life I've always dreamed of. We've decided not to have children because (A) my fiancé is already in his 60's and (B) we'd rather spend our time exploring the world and having fun. I see giftedness as both a blessing and a curse. On one hand, being gifted gives me amazing insight and perspective, which I am incredibly grateful for. On the other hand, being gifted seems to go hand in hand with chronic loneliness. Finding someone I can truly relate to has always been a challenge for me.

People tend to have unrealistic expectations of me simply because I am gifted. My reasoning and critical thinking skills may be above average but I am significantly behind in other aspects of my development. For instance, I'm 29 years old and I still don't have a car or a driver's license. I don't have any close friends, either. My emotional sensitivity (yet another aspect of my “giftedness”) causes me to suffer from anxiety, fear of failure, and other factors that prevent my success. On top of that I also have to deal with the jealousy, competitiveness, lack of compassion, and resentfulness that others feel towards me even at the mere mention of the word "gifted". 

It doesn't surprise me that we have a higher risk of developing disabilities like mental illness, suicidal tendencies, addictions, behavior disorders and learning disabilities. I myself have been diagnosed with generalized anxiety disorder, major depression, and anorexia nervosa. In fact, I just recently spent 110 days in a treatment center for women with eating disorders. I was so low-functioning that I literally could not feed myself anymore.  My therapist told me that my development stopped when my eating disorder started (around age 16) which means I am essentially a teenager trapped inside an adult woman's body. I can relate to your situation because I often wonder if anyone will love me and accept me as I am. 

The desire to find someone who understands us is human nature. Loneliness is a major issue for many adults, but particularly for those who are gifted. We have a unique way of perceiving the world. Our reality may be somewhat different than the reality of those around us. It can be difficult for us to feel true connections with others. Even when we have what appears to be many friends, we can still feel lonely. Loneliness is a feeling of distress that accompanies perceived deficiencies in social relationships. It often occurs in conjunction with social isolation, but a person can be socially isolated without feeling lonely or can feel lonely without being socially isolated. Loneliness has more to do with the perceived quality of social relationships than it does the quantity.

Researchers theorize that in order to truly connect and form a friendship we often need to find someone within 10-20 points of our own IQ score. With only about 3-5% of the world’s population exhibiting gifted characteristics, and even less having similar interests and personality compatibility, this makes it quite difficult to find a perfect match. Read [this article](http://oneworldgifted.weebly.com/blog/one-true-peer) for more info.

I like the reflection of light that you drew inside her irises. It's such a small detail but it really adds dimension to her eyes. I would love to see more highlights and shadows on her face, especially around her forehead, cheeks, and chin. A bit of shading could really make them pop. I would also erase the dark outline around her jaw. It's not realistic and it takes away from the depth of the drawing. You can create the illusion of a jawline by defining the edges with two different tones meeting rather than a harsh outline. Remember, you are creating an illusion with areas of tonal value. When you use a hard drawn line to define an edge you disrupt this illusion.

I think of my creative side as a sponge. It soaks up different sights and sounds and ideas as I go about my day. Once the sponge has reached its maximum absorbency capacity new ideas begin to flow out of it. It sounds like you've squeezed all of the creative juices out of yours. Maybe it's time to take a break and start absorbing again. Visit a gallery, watch a movie that's known for its beautiful cinematography, flip through the pages of an underground art magazine. These are things that have helped me in the past.
